--- title: "Bikeshare_SpaceTime_Prediction" subtitle: "CPLN 5080 - Spring 2026" author: "Jenny" date: today format: html: code-fold: show code-tools: true toc: true toc-depth: 3 toc-location: left theme: cosmo embed-resources: true editor: visual execute: warning: false message: false --- # INTRODUCTION ## The Rebalancing Challenge in Philadelphia Philadelphia's Indego bike share system faces the same operational challenge as every bike share system: **rebalancing bikes to meet anticipated demand**. Considering there are 200 stations across Philadelphia, limited trucks and staff for moving bikes, and 2-3 hours before morning rush hour demand peaks. **The question:** this report is grounded in are if stations will run out of bikes by 8:30 AM? This report builds predictive models that forecast bike share demand across space (different stations) and time (different hours) to help solve this problem. The first part of the report explores data from Q1 2025 (January through March) and tests various temporal, weather, demographic, and spatial features to find the best model for predicting hourly trip demand at the station level. Through a series of progressively more complex linear models, we identify which predictors drive the most improvement in forecast accuracy. The second part applies the same workflowto Q4 2025 (October through December), which had interesting weather patterns, warm October followed by a cold snap in mid-December, as well as notable holidays including Thanksgiving, and Christmas. Three additional features were engineered, specifically holiday indicators, a nice weather feature, and distance to the nearest bike lane. By comparing the first part of the year to the last, this report aim to understand how seasons shape ridership behaviour and model performance, if predictors that matter most in winter carry over to fall, and what the error patterns reveal about which communities and time periods are hardest to predict. If there were 15 bike trips from Station A at 8:00 AM, there will probably be \~15 trips at 9:00 AM. We can use this temporal persistence to improve predictions. **Note:** We still can't use spatial lags in prediction. Temporal lags are different because time moves in one direction - past predicts the future, but the future does not predict the past. Spatial lags are non-directional and create circular prediction logic. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Sort by station and time study_panel <- study_panel %>% arrange(start_station, interval60) # Create lag variables WITHIN each station study_panel <- study_panel %>% group_by(start_station) %>% mutate( lag1Hour = lag(Trip_Count, 1), lag2Hours = lag(Trip_Count, 2), lag3Hours = lag(Trip_Count, 3), lag12Hours = lag(Trip_Count, 12), lag1day = lag(Trip_Count, 24) ) %>% ungroup() # Remove rows with NA lags (first 24 hours for each station) study_panel_complete <- study_panel %>% filter(!is.na(lag1day)) cat("Rows after removing NA lags:", format(nrow(study_panel_complete), big.mark = ","), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows after removing NA lags: 520,870 ``` ::: ::: ## Visualize Lag Correlations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # The rush hour interaction in Model 5 added marginal improvement at 0.361. \ The three new features engineered for Q4 included holidays, nice weather, and bike lane distance, and were all statistically significant. Holidays reduced expected trip counts by about 0.062 trips per station-hour (p<0.001), while nice weather days increased them by 0.048 (p<0.001), and each additional foot of distance from a bike lane reduced trips by a small but significant amount. Despite this statistical significance, neither Model 6 nor Model 7 substantially improved MAE over Model 2, suggesting that the temporal lag structure is better prediction accuracy and the new features explain variance without dramatically sharpening forecasts. The Poisson model produced a dispersion of 1.47 (mild overdispersion) and performed similarly to Model 2 for MAE. The most notable finding is how similar Q4 and Q1 model performance is despite the seasonal differences. Both quarters produce their best MAE of roughly 0.41 under Model 2, and ordering of model improvements is roughly the same. This suggests the underlying space-time prediction framework works well across seasons. That said, Q4 R² values are slightly higher than Q1 across all equivalent models. For example, Model 2 has R² = 0.329 in Q4 versus 0.229 in Q1. This could reflects Q4 demand being more dominated by regular commuting patterns as recreational riders drop off in colder weather, making demand easier to explain with time and weather predictors alone. Q1 by contrast includes the Eagles Super Bowl parade on February 14th, an possible outlier that increases this unexplained variance. ## Critical Reflection ###Operational implications The best model achieves an MAE of approximately 0.41 trips per station-hour. However, it is hard to determing if this is "good enough"; it will depend on the operational context. For low-demand overnight hours, an error of 0.41 trips is negligible. For rush-hour stations in Center City that average 2–3 trips per hour, this represents roughly a 15–20% error, which could meaningfully affect rebalancing decisions. We would recommend deploying this system with human oversight rather than as a fully automated rebalancing tool. The model is most reliable for routine weekday commuting patterns and least reliable for high-demand stations during special events or unusual weather. A deployment strategy that flags high-uncertainty predictions for manual review would be best. analysis shows that prediction errors are higher in wealthier, whiter neighborhoods and lower in transit-dependent communities. This means automated rebalancing based on these predictions would be most reliable where demand is commuter-driven and least reliable in areas with more recreational or event-based riding. One concern is if errors are proportionally similar across neighborhoods, lower-income stations have lower absolute demand, so any kinbd of misallocation of bikes matters more at the margin. Safeguards should include monitoring outcomes by neighborhood income level, ensuring that stations in lower-income areas are not systematically deprioritized when predictions are uncertain, and supplementing algorithmic decisions with local knowledge from operations people familiar with community patterns. ### limitations The model's most significant gap is its inability to capture certain special events like concerts, sports games, protests, and festivals. These create large unpredictable demand spikes in specific stations. It also cannot account for changes in the Indego system itself, where, for example, a new stations opening or capacity changes. With more time and data, incorporating real-time event calendars and station capacity data could likely yeild the most meaningful improvements.
